deliverable.name: A colleague from accounting gets from a fresh terminal to a client's printed invoice by the guide alone

goal: The user lets their accounting team print each client's invoice themselves, from the invoice lines they keep in a LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet and at that client's tax rate, without writing Python. Once it holds, a colleague from accounting, on their Linux laptop, follows a guide to run one invoicer command in a terminal on their spreadsheet's lines with the client's tax rate, and gets the invoice printed, with no one writing code for them.

decisions.decided: Someone who has never run invoicer follows the guide alone on a Linux machine with python3 and LibreOffice: they save a sheet of lines, run each command the guide gives, in order, with a client's tax rate, and get that client's invoice with the subtotal, tax, and total counted by hand. Shown by running the guide's commands in order on a fresh copy of the folder and a sheet laid out as the guide says.
After the invoice shows in the terminal and its totals are checked, the guide gives the same command ending in `| lp` to send it to the laptop's default printer.
One command turns the spreadsheet the user keeps into the client's invoice, at the tax rate given with it.

S1: As a colleague from accounting, I get a client's invoice from the lines in my spreadsheet, at that client's tax rate. S2: As a colleague from accounting, when my sheet or rate is wrong, I learn what to fix before any invoice comes out.

The command shows the invoice in the terminal, so the user checks the lines and totals on screen; the guide then gives the one command that sends the same invoice to their printer. The command itself never sends anything to a printer.
S1 carries O1 and KR1.1; S2 carries KR1.1 and KR1.2, as a wrong invoice caught early costs neither a reprint nor a developer's time. P1 to P3 trace to the ideas of the vision's concept.

P1 The sheet as they keep it: the command reads the .ods file saved from Calc, its first sheet, with a header row naming the columns. P2 No wrong invoice: the command checks the whole sheet and the rate before it writes any line of the invoice, and a refusal names the row and column or the argument to fix. P3 Nothing to install: the command uses Python's standard library alone and runs as `python3 -m invoicer` from the invoicer folder.

The command takes the spreadsheet's path and the tax rate, and hands back the invoice or a refusal. The sheet reader turns the .ods file into the invoice's lines, and alone knows the file's layout. The existing render, tax, and totals parts make the invoice's text from the lines and the rate, unchanged.

The .ods layout and the columns belong to the sheet reader; the form of the arguments, the percentage, and what a refusal looks like belong to the command; the invoice's text layout stays with render.
Each component is a Python module of the invoicer package; the command is the package's `__main__` module, run as `python3 -m invoicer`.

The spreadsheet holds one or more lines of one invoice. The tax rate is one for each invoice. The invoice holds each line, its subtotal, its tax at the rate, and its total. A refusal names one fault of the spreadsheet or the rate.

decisions.about: the sequence of S1 and S2
decisions.decided: The user runs the command with the spreadsheet's path and the rate; the command checks the rate; the command asks the sheet reader for the lines; the sheet reader reads the .ods file and gives the lines; the command hands the lines and the rate to render, which gives the invoice's text; the command writes it out. Where the rate or the sheet is wrong, the command writes the refusal to the terminal's error output and ends with a failing status, and writes no invoice.
The stories, principles, components, data, and sequence name the same parts and the same .ods file, rate, and invoice.

The user's Linux laptop, with python3 3.9 or later, LibreOffice Calc, and its printer set up through CUPS, runs the command from the invoicer folder on a spreadsheet file kept on the laptop; the guide's `lp` sends the shown invoice to that printer. GitHub's CI runs the tests. No other service is needed.

invoicer/: the package, with __main__.py for the command and sheet.py for the sheet reader beside the existing modules. tests/: the unit and integration tests, which build their .ods files themselves. docs/print-an-invoice.md: the accounting team's guide.

Unit tests with Python's unittest try the sheet reader and the command against their contracts, during the work. Integration tests run `python3 -m invoicer` as a process on .ods files that the tests build, for each path of the sequence, during the work. An end-to-end check follows the guide's commands on a fresh copy of the folder and compares the invoice with totals counted by hand, before sign-off. Criterion: every test passes on each run. The trace: each story, principle item, component, and data has an integration test.
No gap of the software design or the test design is known yet; each one found goes back into this design before the code is made.

decisions.about: the parts that hold each behavior
decisions.decided: Reading the sheet: the sheet reader. Taking and checking the rate, refusing, and writing out: the command. The invoice's text and sums: render, tax, and totals. Each is a module that a unit test calls.

The .ods file is read with zipfile and xml.etree of the standard library (P1, P3). Money stays Decimal from the cell's value to the total (S1). The rate is given as a percentage, such as 19 for 19 %, and becomes the fraction that tax_of takes (S1). The checks of P2 run before render is called (S2).
Only what holds while the vision and the principles stay; module names appear in the folders alone.
